title: The Amazonian Trap: How Heteropessimism Is Harming Young Women
gist: The authors argue young American women are adopting an 'Amazonian' strategy of detachment from men — 39% of single women under 40 aren't looking for a relationship and over 80% of eligible women in their 20s and 30s aren't dating seriously — and that this is a trap, since GSS data show unmarried childless women aged 25-39 are nearly three times more likely to be unhappy than married mothers the same age. They relay life coach Suzanne Venker's three counter-cultural guideposts (marry 'youngish', declare intentions within three dates, choose a flexible career) and rebut Matt Yglesias's charge that this amounts to suppressing women's ambition.

insights.claim: Only 24% of American women aged 18-29 believe married mothers are ultimately happier than other women — far lower than any other demographic group.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A collapse in the perceived value of marriage among the cohort that drives future household formation — the belief precedes the behaviour.
insights.quote: Only 24% of women 18–29 believe "married mothers are ultimately happier than other women," far lower than any other group.
insights.locator: This pessimism is reflected in young women's declining faith

insights.claim: The share of US high school girls expecting to marry has fallen from more than 80% in 2010 to just 67% today.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Marriage expectations are dropping before the dating years even begin — a leading indicator for the marriage rate 10-15 years out.
insights.quote: In 2010, more than 80% expected to marry; now it's just 67%.
insights.locator: High school girls' hopes for marriage are also retreating

insights.claim: Pew found 39% of single US women under 40 are not even looking for a relationship, and IFS/Wheatley Institute research shows more than 80% of eligible women in their 20s and 30s are not dating anyone seriously — what the authors call a 'dating recession'.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Demand-side collapse for dating apps and relationship services: the addressable market is opting out rather than switching platforms.
insights.quote: Pew found 39% of single women under 40 aren't even looking for a relationship at all

insights.claim: General Social Survey data show unmarried, childless women in their 20s and 30s are nearly three times more likely to be unhappy with their lives than married mothers aged 25-39.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: The central empirical claim underpinning the pronatalist policy push; the 3x happiness gap is the number that will be cited in the debate.
insights.quote: Unmarried, childless women in their 20s and 30s are nearly three times more likely to be unhappy with their lives compared to married mothers the same age (25-39), according to the General Social Survey.
insights.locator: But the apostles of women going their own way

insights.claim: The behavioural markers of the trend are specific and observable: deleting dating apps, posting 'boy sober' TikToks, Sunday brunches with female friends only, and hardening conviction that men are more trouble than they're worth.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Concrete consumer-behaviour signals to track — dating-app churn and 'boy sober' content volume are measurable proxies for the trend.
insights.quote: They're doing it by deleting dating apps, posting "boy sober" TikToks, enjoying Sunday brunches spent with just female friends
insights.locator: Millennia later, many young American women

insights.claim: The authors identify influencer economics as a driver, arguing influencers get clicks by painting men and marriage in the worst possible light alongside mainstream media depictions of men as emotionally and socially stunted 'child-men'.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Attention-economy incentives are proposed as a causal input to declining family formation — a monetisation loop that will not self-correct.
insights.locator: They are discouraged by mainstream media depictions of men

insights.claim: Life coach and author Suzanne Venker reports that 30-something women arriving at her office are desperate to start or sustain a family but have no idea how, having spent their 20s building the scaffolding of independence — careers, savings, status — exactly as second-wave feminism scripted.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Clinical-practice evidence of a systematic timing mismatch; the demand is for guidance and services aimed at the 20s, not the 30s.
insights.locator: Perhaps that explains why so many hurting women in their 30s

insights.claim: The core mechanism the authors identify is non-reversibility: by the time women feel ready in their 30s the switch does not flip on command, because the pool of good men in their immediate circles has shrunk, pivoting from career and travel to marriage and young kids is unexpectedly hard, and pregnancy is difficult or impossible for some in their late 30s.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Frames family formation as a path-dependent option that expires — the argument that will drive policy toward earlier-life interventions.
insights.quote: The Amazonian detachment they leaned into in their 20s, it turns out, does not reverse itself just because a woman decides she's finally ready for a family.
insights.locator: By the time they feel "ready" in their 30s

insights.claim: Venker frames her own outreach problem as a timing failure she cannot solve: 'I'm trying to get to you when you're 22 before you come to me at 32. But at 22, you're not interested, and at 32, you're like, help me, help me.'
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: The demand for this advice materialises exactly when it can no longer be acted on — a structural obstacle to any behavioural intervention here.
insights.quote: The running joke is, well, I’m trying to get to you when you’re 22 before you come to me at 32. But at 22, you’re not interested, and at 32, you’re like, help me, help me.
insights.locator: In Venker's words, the "choice to marry young(ish)"

insights.claim: Venker's first guidepost is to be open to marrying 'youngish' — mid to late 20s — because the husband hunt gets harder after 30 and college is the biggest dating pool some women will ever encounter, with the stated benefits being a better dating pool, strong fertility and faster wealth building.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: An explicit search-market argument: pool density peaks in college and decays afterwards, which is the mechanism behind the timing advice.
insights.quote: choice to marry young(ish) has so many benefits—a better dating pool, strong fertility, the opportunity to build wealth faster
insights.locator: First, if you find a good guy, be open to marrying

insights.claim: Venker's second guidepost is to date with intention and get expectations about family, career and commitment level on the table within the first three dates, because 'there's just so much pretending going on' in modern dating.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Prescribes early information disclosure to cut search costs — the same logic as reducing asymmetric information in any matching market.
insights.quote: Just get it out on the table in the first three dates
insights.locator: Second, she recommends dating with intention

insights.claim: Venker's third guidepost is to choose a career that complements rather than competes with future family plans — favouring roles that can be done part-time or from home such as nursing and teaching classically, or financial advising and consulting more recently — rather than an expensive degree that locks in a decade or more of debt just as priorities shift.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Names specific occupations as family-compatible, an implicit bet on flexible and freelance-capable professional services over debt-financed credentialing.
insights.quote: Rather than putting career at the center of your life and trying to fit men and marriage and motherhood in around that
insights.locator: Third, Venker says women who are particularly family-minded

insights.claim: Venker advises assessing a prospective husband's character and professional possibilities — not his wealth but his reliability as a provider — on the grounds that a wife generally needs a man she can depend on financially at least for a short period while stepping back to raise young children.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Reliability over income level as the screening criterion — relevant to how household financial planning products are positioned to this cohort.
insights.quote: a man on whom you can depend financially (even) if only for a short period
insights.locator: If family matters to you, figure out

insights.claim: 71% of Americans believe a man should be able to provide for his family while only 32% say the same of women, a gap Venker reads as instinctive public recognition that women become vulnerable when they have a child.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: A 39-point asymmetry in provider expectations persists despite decades of egalitarian norms — durable demand for male-earnings-based household models.
insights.quote: That says to me that we know instinctively that women become vulnerable when they have a child
insights.locator: She points to a telling gap in public opinion

insights.claim: The authors rebut journalist Matt Yglesias's theory that family-first conservatives like Venker really want to suppress women's ambition, arguing the charge shortchanges the word 'ambition' by relegating it to the marketplace alone.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Shows how the pronatalist camp is repositioning its argument to neutralise the anti-feminist critique — the rhetorical frame to expect in this debate.
insights.quote: Why do we call a woman's hunger for a high-status career "ambition," but not her hunger for a rich and meaningful family life?

insights.claim: The authors' central claim is that most women end up ambitious for family life even when also ambitious for intellectual and professional life, and that women who build families with men in marriage are among the happiest in the country.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: The revealed-preference argument that supports the whole piece; if true, the current dating recession is a temporary preference-expression failure rather than a permanent shift.
insights.locator: However regressive some commentators find it

insights.claim: The authors argue that to date with marriage in mind and to choose a career with a future family in mind is now to swim upstream against a culture that prizes Amazonian detachment.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Frames family-oriented planning as counter-cultural, which means adoption will require deliberate institutional support rather than drift.
insights.quote: In this culture, to date with marriage in mind, and to choose a career with a future family in mind, is to swim upstream.
insights.locator: In essence, Venker is asking young women

insights.claim: The authors point to a Hollywood actress feted in The New York Times for declaring herself 'choicefully single, happily, gloriously single' as the elite-media emblem of the women-going-their-own-way position they are contesting.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Illustrates the prestige-media reinforcement channel the authors blame — useful for tracking where the cultural narrative is set.
insights.locator: But the apostles of women going their own way

insights.claim: The article was first published in Deseret News and reprinted by the Institute for Family Studies with permission, with Brad Wilcox identified as Distinguished University Professor of Sociology at the University of Virginia and IFS senior fellow.
insights.speaker: Maria Baer and Brad Wilcox
insights.so_what: Maps the syndication path by which IFS positions reach a mainstream audience — the distribution mechanism behind the pronatalist narrative's reach.
insights.locator: Editor's Note: This article appeared first at Deseret News
